name: The One (Parmenidean Being)
plain_explanation: Parmenides held that behind all the changing things we perceive with our senses, there is really only one single, unchanging, indivisible thing -- 'the One' -- and that our impression of a changing multiplicity of things is an illusion produced by unreliable senses.
precise_definition: The sole true reality in Parmenides' metaphysics: infinite, indivisible, and (though apparently conceived as material and extended, even spherical) not composed of parts or opposites, since Parmenides denies that opposites (e.g. hot/cold, light/dark) are anything more than the presence or absence of a single quality.
why_it_mattered: Introduces, for the first time in the tradition Russell is tracing, a fully worked-out metaphysics of unchanging Being set logically against Heraclitus's flux, and supplies the ancestor of the philosophical concept of substance that dominates Western metaphysics, psychology, physics, and theology for over two thousand years.
historical_origin: Set out in Parmenides' poem On Nature, divided into 'the way of truth' and 'the way of opinion'.
examples: Parmenides' description of the One as a kind of sphere, present as a whole everywhere and therefore indivisible
objections: Russell's own objection: the argument rests on the false assumption that words have a wholly constant meaning, ignoring that the same name can correspond to different mental content for different speakers or at different times
competing_positions: Heraclitus's doctrine of universal flux and the many
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly shapes Plato's doctrines (via a reported meeting with Socrates); more generally introduces the idea, retained by 'subsequent philosophy down to quite modern times', of 'the indestructibility of substance' as the persistent subject of varying predicates.
